intros.intro:
An agent can go wrong not only by wanting the wrong thing but by moving too freely while it learns. This page gathers two of Concrete Problems' remedies, for side effects and for unsafe exploration, that both work by narrowing what an agent may touch or try, rather than by rewriting its reward.

Seven themes trace that shared strategy: baseline-distance and influence-limiting penalties for side effects, then risk-sensitive policies and recoverable-region constraints for exploration, with formal verification and demonstration learning running underneath both. Four super edges tie these threads together, and sources into the paper follow.

A proxy standing in for a goal will eventually diverge from that goal once it gets optimized directly, and this page follows that pattern surfacing across three papers written six years apart. It traces Concrete Problems' account of how reward proxies get gamed, and the two families of fix the paper proposes for it.

The walk moves from the anatomy of reward hacking to two remedies, one adversarial and borrowed from GAN training, one built from ordinary software safeguards like sandboxing and trip wires, before closing on Goodhart's law itself, the single principle both remedies answer. Five super edges connect these four themes, and sources follow.

Checking an AI system's every output by hand does not scale, and this page follows what happened to that problem over six years: a 2016 sketch of possible fixes, and the working training pipeline InstructGPT eventually built out of one of them.

Eight themes carry the story from Concrete Problems' open problem and its two proposed remedies, through the reward model and AI feedback that grew out of them, into InstructGPT's pretrain-finetune-reward-PPO pipeline and the labeling work behind it, ending with where that pipeline still falls short. Seven super edges link the themes, and sources follow.

A model trained on one distribution of data will eventually meet another, and Concrete Problems treats that mismatch as its own open problem with more than one kind of answer. This page follows two of those answers side by side.

The narrative first weakens the statistics connecting training and test data, through importance weighting and partial specification, then abandons that framing for causal reasoning and software-style contracts on a model's assumptions, with formal verification supplying a shared toolkit underneath both. Three super edges and a set of sources close out the page.

Before it reaches any technical remedy, Concrete Problems spends real effort saying what it is not about. This page follows that framing work, done once at the paper's opening and once again near its close.

It moves from the paper distinguishing accidents from superintelligence risk, through the boundary it draws against six adjacent fields like privacy and fairness, to the formal-methods toolkit that gives an old idea, Asimov's first law, a rigor it never had on its own. Two super edges connect these three themes, and sources follow.

Claiming a model is more aligned takes more than saying so; it takes more than one kind of measurement. This page follows the battery of instruments InstructGPT assembles to check quality, capability, and safety all at once.

It moves from the two basic families of metric, overlap scores like ROUGE and BLEU against judgment-based scores like win rate and Elo, through the public benchmarks used to catch any loss in general capability, to the purpose-built tests for truthfulness and bias that neither family could have caught. Three super edges and sources close the page.

Before InstructGPT could optimize for being aligned, it had to say what that word meant, and this page follows that definitional work across two papers. Predicting the next word, it turns out, is the wrong thing to train for, and something else has to take its place.

The narrative moves from instruction-following as InstructGPT's proposed replacement objective, through the helpful-honest-harmless vocabulary it shares with Constitutional AI, to the tension between helpfulness and harmlessness that pursuing the target in practice creates, and the metric used to track it. Four super edges and sources follow.

Constitutional AI trains a model to critique and revise its own harmful answers using a short written constitution instead of human harm labels, and this page follows that method from its supervised stage through to the systems it was built against.

It moves from the constitution-driven critique-and-revision stage, through the prompting and calibration work needed to turn a model into a usable preference labeler, to the red-teamed data both stages consume, closing with the prior dialogue agents, LaMDA and Sparrow among them, the paper positions itself relative to. Four super edges and sources follow.

A single 2016 principle can take years to earn a name, and this page follows Goodhart's law as it turns up, unnamed, in two different 2022 papers before Constitutional AI finally calls it by that term.

Four edges carry the thread: from the abstract statement of the law to InstructGPT's reward-model over-optimization, down to a single hedging subfeature, and across to Constitutional AI's evasiveness, where the proxy was miscorrelated from the start rather than decorrelating under optimization. Sources into all three papers follow.

Some ideas in this corpus come in pairs: the same underlying structure, run toward opposite ends. This page collects seven such pairs, from opposite sides of an attack to opposite grammatical moods of the same written constitution.

The walk moves through security and abuse as mirror images, empowerment minimized rather than maximized, and inverted legibility between an agent and the human it learns from, closing on two InstructGPT failure modes, hedging and evasiveness, and hallucination and hedging, that sit at opposite ends of a single dial. Sources follow.

Not every safety mechanism in Concrete Problems is designed from scratch. This page follows two remedies for side effects, the impact regularizer and penalize-influence, each stitched together out of borrowed pieces, with a mismatch flagged wherever a piece doesn't quite fit.

It traces the impact regularizer from an overcorrecting first attempt through borrowed safe regions and improvement guarantees to a transfer-learned variant, then does the same for penalize-influence, from its inverted empowerment measure through a reinterpreted notion of power to a swap of hand-tuned penalty for prior belief. Sources follow.

Concrete Problems regularly reaches into other fields for ready-made tools, and just as often admits the fit is imperfect. This page follows five of those imports and the specific place each one stops transferring cleanly.

It moves from adversarial reward functions borrowing an assumption GANs don't actually share with a reward-seeking agent, through counterexample resistance and adversarial blinding drawing on two different lineages of adversarial machine learning despite sitting side by side, to bounded exploration and partially specified models each generalizing an idea past where it was first proven. Sources follow.

Concrete Problems rarely settles on one fix for a given vulnerability. This page follows several places where it offers a fork instead, two or more remedies for the same gap, distinguished by which layer or timescale each one intervenes at rather than by which is correct.

Ten edges carry the walk, from reward tampering split between foresight and freezing, through adversarial defenses working at different layers and exploration algorithms blind to danger for different reasons, to scalable oversight's own fork between cheaper checks and rarer ones. Sources into the underlying papers follow.

Timing turns out to matter as much as the fix itself: whether a safety property is enforced while a system searches for a policy, or repaired afterward once it is already trained. This page follows a cluster of paired ideas in Concrete Problems' distributional-shift section built around exactly that distinction.

The walk moves from counterfactual reasoning and machine learning with contracts as descriptive and prescriptive counterparts, through reachability analysis acting ex ante during search, to model repair as its ex post counterpart, restored after training is already done. Sources follow.

Concrete Problems is unusually candid about where its own proposed remedies run out. This page follows seven places the paper flags a limit in its own solution, rather than leaving the reader to find the gap.

It moves through a theoretically correct but impractical fix for partially observed goals, formal verification's admitted blind spot toward modern machine learning, and wireheading's structural cause, which can only be mitigated rather than removed, closing with careful engineering's own admission that it cannot catch every bug. Sources follow.

Partially specified models start from a single worked example in Concrete Problems, and this page follows how far that one idea gets stretched once the paper's own citations are read closely.

The walk moves from covariate shift's untestable assumption motivating a retreat to partial specification generally, through the generalized method of moments aiming at parameter identification, to unsupervised risk estimation asking a different question, how wrong a model is, rather than what the right one would be. Sources follow.

InstructGPT and Constitutional AI lean on existing benchmarks rather than building new ones, and this page follows several places where reusing a benchmark quietly changed what it measures.

It moves from a bias-entropy metric that strips direction out of Winogender and CrowS-Pairs, through a Winograd Schema variant that no longer matches its own leaderboard's format, to the Perspective API's proprietary definition of toxicity, and closes with the HHH evaluation set's own forking history once models began to saturate it. Sources follow.

A few of InstructGPT's benchmarks quietly change role partway through the paper, from neutral evaluation to the thing a training run is actually tuned against. This page follows that promotion and what it does to the claim that the alignment tax got fixed.

The walk moves through SQuAD and DROP as the shared regression testbed for two separate coefficient sweeps, Hellaswag escaping a regression that persists in DROP, and translation bearing a tax that summarization is spared, closing with F1 score demoted from a quality measure to a regression alarm. Sources follow.

InstructGPT's PPO objective looks like a single reward from the outside, but it is really a small system of interacting design choices. This page follows how those pieces, a KL penalty, a bandit formulation, a pretraining mix, work on each other.

It moves from the KL penalty countering reward over-optimization and densifying an otherwise sparse bandit reward, through the bandit setting itself rendering discounting moot, to the paper keeping this term separate from a second knob, PPO-ptx, that fixes capability loss without touching the alignment gain. Sources follow.

The corpus rarely trusts a single metric on its own; a primary measurement is usually paired with a second, independently sourced check, and this page follows where the two agree and where they quietly diverge.

Nine edges trace that pairing: win rate checked against inter-annotator agreement, Likert ratings, and Elo score, Elo itself cross-checked by an absolute harmfulness score, safety measures diverging from each other under respectful prompting, and a structural blind spot in reward-model loss that leaves its scale undefined until the paper imposes one by convention. Sources follow.

Constitutional AI's headline result did not arrive as a single number; it was built step by step, and this page follows that construction edge by edge.

The walk moves from the helpfulness-harmlessness tension collapsing into evasiveness, through the RLHF baseline the paper measures itself against, to RL-CAI redesigning what gets rewarded to eliminate that evasiveness and land above the old tradeoff line, closing with the admission that the Elo score used to show this was itself tuned to penalize the behavior. Sources follow.

A handful of techniques in this corpus get asked to do more than one job, and comparing those jobs side by side is where this page's interest lies.

It follows inverse reinforcement learning doing double duty against reward hacking and unsafe exploration, cooperative inverse reinforcement learning solving both the shutdown problem and a demonstration-learning problem as a side effect of its own structure, and principle ensembling paying off differently depending on which training stage it is applied at. Sources follow.

Constitutional AI's feedback model depends on a chain of narrow prompting and formatting choices, each one load-bearing for the step after it. This page follows that chain from calibration to prompt.

The walk moves from model calibration enabling a multiple-choice comparison format, through that format turning an ordinary language model into a preference labeler, to chain-of-thought prompting creating an overconfidence problem that then has to be corrected by clamping labels into a narrow band. Sources follow.

A recurring move across this corpus swaps an AI process in for a human one at precisely the point human throughput was running short, leaving everything around it unchanged. This page follows that substitution as it recurs at several different stages.

It moves from RLHF's labeler being swapped for RLAIF's feedback model, through the constitution replacing tens of thousands of human comparisons with roughly ten written principles, back to Concrete Problems anticipating the same shape six years earlier, and closing with red teaming scaling into its automated form. Sources follow.

These papers argue as much through concrete examples as through abstract claims, and this page checks how much weight each example actually carries, sometimes exactly as intended and sometimes more than it should.

It moves from the cleaning-robot example deliberately reused across every problem type in Concrete Problems, through an evolved-radio anecdote that turns out to retroactively fit a taxonomy introduced a page later, to two accidental cases in InstructGPT: duplicated training templates and a results-table row copied across two supposedly independent benchmarks. Sources follow.

Concrete Problems does not leave scalable oversight as a philosophical worry; it turns the idea into concrete, combinable experimental machinery. This page follows that machinery being assembled piece by piece.

The walk moves from semi-supervised reinforcement learning turning an oversight budget into a literal labeled-fraction dial, through Atari and bAbI proposed as graded testbeds for exactly that dial, to active reward learning and unsupervised value iteration drawing complementary signals from the same pool of unlabeled episodes at once. Sources follow.

Neither training pipeline in this corpus passes data through untouched; specific filtering, sampling, and interface choices at each stage shape exactly what the next stage can learn from. This page follows that shaping, stage by stage.

It moves through the SFT dataset training the very policies the reward-model dataset later samples from, a labeling interface that filters uncertain comparisons out before training ever sees them, and closes with Constitutional AI's own chain: critique-and-revision feeding SL-CAI, SL-CAI seeding RL-CAI, and red-teamed transcripts feeding the paper's harm classifiers. Sources follow.

InstructGPT beats a model a hundred times its size, and the paper does not let that claim stand on its own; it builds a ladder of comparisons showing exactly which asymmetry the win comes from. This page follows that ladder rung by rung.

It moves from a reward model roughly thirty times smaller than the policy it supervises, through a constitution that substitutes ten written principles for tens of thousands of human comparisons, to three instruction-tuned baselines, T0, FLAN, and a prompted GPT-3, each isolating a different reason the previous one falls short. Sources follow.

Both training pipelines in this corpus look like a strictly forward sequence in their own diagrams, but several of their artifacts quietly do more than one job, or send causality running backward. This page follows those loops.

The walk moves from a reward model that back-selects which SFT checkpoint precedes it, through an SFT model filling two separate roles, initialization and reference, with two different checkpoints, to a prompt distribution that Constitutional AI's own supervised data helped bring into existence in the first place. Sources follow.

Concrete Problems is careful to say what it is choosing not to cover, and this page follows four of those explicit exclusions.

It moves from the paper's narrowing away from long-term AI-risk framing, through the shutdown problem flagged as exceeding the paper's own single-agent frame even as the same section introduces it, to wireheading marked as narrower than reward hacking in general, and privacy's contrast with security research. Sources follow.

Several ideas in this corpus have an older ancestor, a decades-old piece of scholarship that named or foreshadowed the problem informally before any of these papers gave it technical treatment. This page follows four of those ancestries.

It moves from Asimov's first law as an unmechanized precursor to accidents in machine learning, through the 1969 frame problem resurfacing largely unaddressed in reward design, to formal verification showing what rigorous harm-avoidance actually looks like, and closes with a 2011 result, the delusion box, that already modeled wireheading's core failure. Sources follow.

Eight connections in this corpus exist only in hindsight: neither paper states the link itself, and it becomes visible only once a later paper is read against an earlier one. This page follows those seams.

It moves from Goodhart's law fragmenting into reward over-optimization, hedging, and evasiveness across two 2022 papers, through demonstrations becoming supervised fine-tuning with the reward-inference machinery quietly dropped, to scalable oversight being retroactively matched to the reward model, a link only Constitutional AI's own framing makes visible. Sources follow.

Three failures in this corpus trace back to the data or the labeling instructions rather than to any optimizer setting, and each one gets repaired in the same place it broke. This page follows all three.

The walk moves from evasiveness, fixed by changing what crowdworkers were asked to prefer rather than by tightening the KL penalty, through hedging surfacing because a reward model faithfully optimized labels that genuinely preferred hedged text, to a false-premise failure that shares hedging's fix without sharing its cause. Sources follow.

A source paper's own list or footnote sometimes places two things side by side as if they were equivalent, and a closer look shows they are not. This page follows four such near-misses.

It moves from security and abuse framed as mirror images by one footnote, through privacy's contrast with security that the same footnote's phrasing almost obscures, to adversarial blinding and counterexample resistance sharing only a label, and closes with LaMDA and Sparrow, named together in Constitutional AI's related work while playing functionally unrelated roles. Sources follow.

A conservative baseline computed by one technique repeatedly turns into the literal boundary a second technique is checked against, in both papers' safe-exploration and impact-control sections. This page follows that dependency chain.

It moves from demonstrations supplying the baseline that bounded exploration explores around, through trusted policy oversight delegating a recoverability judgment to a second, more conservative policy, to reachability analysis defining the safe set an impact regularizer later borrows, and closes with InstructGPT's SFT model anchoring PPO training the same way, six years on. Sources follow.

Two edges in this corpus, six years apart, make the identical critique: a method can be proven or trained to near-optimality and still miss the point, because the target it was optimized for is itself under dispute. This page follows both.

It moves from R-max, proven near-optimal only on expected total reward, exactly what risk-sensitive criteria argues is the wrong measure, to GPT-3's next-token objective, optimized about as well as scale allows, while InstructGPT argues the objective itself, not the model's competence, was the problem all along. Sources follow.

This telling follows the corpus in publication order: one diagnosis in 2016, then two attempts at treatment in 2022. It is the most direct route through the material, showing which of the earlier paper's ideas got built and which were left alone.

Five chapters follow in order: Concrete Problems' own scope and its unused proposals, reward hacking's arc from 2016 diagnosis to 2022 recurrence, scalable oversight's path into InstructGPT's RLHF pipeline, InstructGPT's target and its measurements, then Constitutional AI's method and result. Open one chapter at a time; the controls above the tree let you zoom from the single claim down to individual concepts.

This telling sets publication order aside and instead follows the order InstructGPT's training pipeline is actually built in: define the target, gather data, train, then evaluate. Concrete Problems' proposals slot in wherever a documented connection places them; what never made it into the pipeline is saved for last.

Seven chapters follow that build order: problem framing, target definition, data collection, reward-model and policy training, reward hacking's place within it, evaluation, and a closing chapter of proposals the pipeline never adopted. Open one chapter at a time; the controls above the tree set whether you're reading the single claim or down at individual concepts.

This telling splits the corpus into two families of fix for one problem, a mis-specified objective: constrain what a system may do, or change what it is trained to want. It follows the second family into a working pipeline and leaves the first stopped at the proposal stage.

Six chapters move from the shared diagnosis, through Concrete Problems' constraint-based remedies and its learning-based seeds, into the pipeline InstructGPT and Constitutional AI actually built and what it cost and gained, closing on distributional shift, the one problem neither family resolves. Open one chapter at a time; the controls above the tree set how much detail you see.

This telling follows one question through the corpus: who, or what, checks the model's output at each stage. It moves from a human writing an example by hand, to a human ranking outputs, to a reward model standing in for that human, to an AI judging against a written constitution.

Seven chapters carry the ladder: reward hacking and Goodhart's law, side effects and safe exploration left aside, demonstrations, preference labels and the reward model, AI feedback and the constitution, how results were measured, and distributional shift, which no rung touches. Open one chapter at a time; the controls above the tree set the zoom.
